hero.title: OrchID-NCD
hero.description: An end-to-end research framework developed at the University of Naples Federico II for ultra-fine-grained visual classification and representation learning of Ophrys species.

vectorSpace.title: Structured Embedding Space
vectorSpace.description: We construct a high-dimensional vector space where morphologically similar Ophrys species cluster together via Supervised Contrastive Learning [8]. This latent representation enables similarity search, outlier detection, and provides the foundation for discovering previously unseen species.

ncd.title: Novel Class Discovery
ncd.description: Standard classifiers operate under a closed-world assumption. Our research tackles Novel Class Discovery [7]: can a model recognize that an unknown Ophrys does not belong to any known species, and group novel entities into meaningful clusters without supervision?

scientific.title: The Ophrys Problem
scientific.content1: The genus Ophrys is one of the most taxonomically challenging orchid groups in the Mediterranean. These orchids use sexual deception to attract species-specific pollinators, producing flowers that mimic female insects through visual cues, scent, and tactile signals [1].
scientific.content2: This extreme specialisation drives rapid morphological divergence and frequent hybridization, resulting in visually ambiguous specimens that challenge even expert botanists. The Ophrys sphegodes complex alone encompasses multiple cryptic taxa with overlapping phenotypic traits [2][3].

journey.title: Experimental Journey
journey.baselines: The first five experiments explored only ResNet18 (Exp 1–3) and ResNet50 (Exp 4–5) on standard train/val/test splits, using a combined dataset of private field photos and internet-sourced images across six Ophrys species of the sphegodes complex: O. exaltata, O. garganica, O. incubacea, O. majellensis, O. sphegodes, and O. sphegodes ssp. sphegodes (Palena population). Experiment 4 introduced 5-fold stratified cross-validation for both architectures, establishing the rigorous evaluation protocol still in use today. ConvNeXt and DINOv2 had not yet been tested.
journey.leakage: MD5 content hashing revealed that the train and test sets shared visually identical images under different filenames — a subtle form of data leakage that artificially inflated metrics and invalidated all results from Exp 1–5. The same Ophrys photograph, downloaded multiple times with different names, was present in both training and test partitions.
journey.preprocessing: The original pipeline applied aggressive center-cropping to a fixed resolution, destroying aspect ratio information. Since ResNet expects 256×512 inputs while ConvNeXt and DINOv2 use 224×224, the same crop produced distorted, information-poor inputs across architectures. We replaced this with letterbox resizing: images are scaled to fit within the target dimensions while preserving aspect ratio, with black padding bands filling the remaining space.
journey.clean: Experiment 6 is a complete restart on a deduplicated clean split with MD5-verified zero overlap between training (2,192 images) and test (300 balanced, 50 per class). For the first time, six architectures — ResNet18, ResNet50, ConvNeXt-Tiny, ConvNeXt-Small, DINOv2-Small, and DINOv2-Base — are evaluated with per-architecture input sizing and 5-fold stratified cross-validation.

model_selection.title: Architecture Comparison
model_selection.description: We benchmark three families of architectures to understand which inductive biases best capture subtle floral differences: ResNet (hierarchical local features via residual connections [4]), ConvNeXt (modernised CNN with large kernels and LayerNorm [5]), and DINOv2 (self-supervised Vision Transformer with global attention, trained on 142M images [6]).

optimization.title: Per-Architecture Recipes
optimization.description: Each architecture receives a tailored training recipe. DINOv2 is fine-tuned via LoRA adapters [9] (rank r=8, alpha=16, dropout=0.1) targeting the query and value projections of all attention layers, updating just ~0.5% of parameters while keeping the backbone frozen. ResNet uses Adam [10], while ConvNeXt and DINOv2 use AdamW with decoupled weight decay [11].

rigor.title: Experimental Rigor
rigor.description: All results are validated through 5-fold stratified cross-validation on a deduplicated clean split. MD5 hashing ensures zero content overlap between training and test sets, eliminating the data leakage that invalidated our preliminary experiments. Early stopping uses patience on val_loss. We evaluated the Generalization Loss criterion [12] but found it terminated training prematurely, before convergence.

augmentation.title: Balanced Augmentation
augmentation.description: Class imbalance is addressed per-fold: the minority class determines the target count, which is multiplied by the number of augmentation transforms (random flips, rotation, color jitter) to produce a balanced dataset where every class has the same number of training images.

exp9.description: Pure Novel Class Discovery setup: O. majellensis is excluded from training and left as a hidden novel class. The model is trained on 5 species and evaluated on all 6, measuring how well it detects the unseen species as 'unknown' through OSR metrics (AUROC, OSCR).
exp9.waiting: Additional models are being trained and will appear here once NCD evaluation is complete.
exp9.negative_result_title: SpHOR Does Not Improve Open-Set Detection
exp9.negative_result: All six architectures fail to significantly detect O. majellensis as a novel class. The best AUROC is 0.497 (ConvNeXt-Tiny), essentially random chance. This is consistent across architectures: simpler models (ConvNeXt) slightly outperform complex ones (DINOv2-Base: 0.332). The results suggest that Spherical Orthogonal Prototypes (SpHOR) do not provide meaningful open-set detection benefits in this ultra-fine-grained domain. This is a publishable negative result — the species are too morphologically similar for prototype-based rejection to work effectively.

future.title: Exp 8: Open-World Recognition (SpHOR + GCD)
future.phase2_intro: Exp 6 trains classifiers with standard Cross-Entropy loss. While effective for classification, CE does not explicitly structure the embedding space — same-class samples may be scattered and different-class samples may overlap. Exp 7 addresses this by applying Supervised Contrastive Learning (SupCon) [8], which reshapes the latent space so that embeddings of the same species cluster together while different species are pushed apart.
future.phase2_how: How SupCon works. For each image (anchor) in a batch, the loss computes cosine similarities against all other images. Same-class pairs are attracted (positive pairs), while different-class pairs are repelled (negative pairs). This is formalised as an InfoNCE objective [13] with a temperature scaling parameter tau. Unlike Triplet Loss, which requires explicit anchor-positive-negative mining, SupCon naturally uses all pair combinations in the batch.
future.phase2_pipeline: Two-phase training. Each fold of Exp 7 consists of two phases: (1) SupCon pretraining — the backbone and a projection head (embedding_dim to 128) are trained with the contrastive loss; the classifier head is ignored. The best model is selected via KNN accuracy (k=1) on validation embeddings. (2) CE fine-tuning — the projection head is discarded, the backbone is frozen, and only the linear classifier head is trained with Cross-Entropy loss at a higher learning rate (0.01).
future.phase2_why_frozen: Why freeze the backbone? If the backbone were updated during CE fine-tuning, gradients from the Cross-Entropy loss would warp the embedding space to maximise class separability at the expense of the contrastive structure learned in Phase 1 [8]. The resulting embeddings would lose the property that morphologically similar species cluster together — a property essential for Novel Class Discovery [7]. Freezing the backbone also reduces the parameter count by 99.5%, meaning Phase 2 converges in fewer than 50 epochs.
future.phase2_params: Hyperparameters. SupCon Phase: temperature tau=0.07. Projection dimension 128. Per-architecture optimizer and LR from the model registry: Adam with LR=0.001 for ResNet; AdamW with LR=0.0001 for ConvNeXt; AdamW with LR=0.0002 for DINOv2 LoRA. Physical batch size 8 (ResNet/ConvNeXt) or 4 (DINOv2) due to 4 GB VRAM; effective batch 32 via gradient accumulation [8]. CE Phase: LR=0.01, Adam, zero weight decay, patience 15 on val_loss [12], maximum 50 epochs.
future.phase2_memory: Memory constraints and SupCon stability. At batch=4 with 6 classes, random sampling frequently yields batches where all samples belong to different species. The InfoNCE objective requires at least one positive pair per anchor — without it, the log-sum-exp over an all-negative similarity matrix produces NaN gradients. We mitigate this through three mechanisms: (1) empty-positive-batch detection returning zero loss, (2) gradient clipping at max_norm=2.0 [12], and (3) safe L2-normalisation with a numerical epsilon. Gradient accumulation (8 steps) ensures each optimiser step aggregates enough positive pairs for stable learning.
future.phase2_dinov2: DINOv2 special case. DINOv2-Base [6] is a Vision Transformer (ViT-B) with 86M parameters. We use Low-Rank Adaptation (LoRA) [9] with rank r=8, alpha=16, dropout=0.1, applied to the query and value projection matrices of all 12 attention layers. This adds only 0.42M trainable parameters (~0.5% of total). During SupCon Phase 1, LoRA adapters and the projection head are trained jointly. In Phase 2, the backbone and LoRA adapters are frozen; only the linear classifier head is trained.
future.phase3: Exp 8 implements an open-world pipeline for recognising and discovering new Ophrys species, building on the SupCon models from Exp 7. The system consists of three phases: (1) Open-Set Recognition (OSR) based on Spherical Orthogonal Prototypes [16] and Extreme Value Theory (OpenMax) [14]; (2) Generalised Category Discovery (GCD) via multi-granularity clustering [17]; (3) incremental addition of new species with CE head fine-tuning on a frozen backbone. The core hypothesis is that the structured embedding space learned by SupCon in Exp 7 — where each species maps to a localised region on the unit hypersphere — provides the geometric foundation for distinguishing known from novel classes, a task that is provably impossible in the degenerate embedding spaces produced by plain CE [15].
future.phase1_embedding: A key design choice is to enforce that the embedding space lies on the surface of a unit hypersphere (L2-normalised outputs). On the hypersphere, cosine similarity equals Euclidean distance up to a monotonic transformation: d(a,b) = 2 - 2cos(theta). More importantly, spherical embeddings guarantee that every point has bounded distance to all others (maximum chord length = 2), making distance thresholds interpretable globally — a property that unnormalised Euclidean spaces lack, where inter-class distances can grow arbitrarily. This bounded geometry is essential for OSR: the maximum possible distance from any class prototype is 2 (the antipodal point), so rejection thresholds are meaningful regardless of which region of the space a test sample falls into.
future.osr_description: We train K spherical orthogonal prototypes — one per species — that lie on the unit hypersphere and are encouraged to be orthogonal via a repulsive loss [16]: L_rep = (1/K(K-1)) sum_{i != j} (cos(theta_ij))^2. Orthogonal prototypes maximise angular coverage, ensuring each species occupies a distinct conical region of the sphere. At inference, we compute distances from a test embedding to each prototype and fit the tail of each per-class distance distribution with a Weibull distribution: f(x; lambda, k) = (k/lambda) (x/lambda)^{k-1} exp(-(x/lambda)^k). The Weibull CDF models the probability that a sample belongs to the extreme tail of a known class — samples beyond the 95th percentile of all per-class fits are candidate unknowns. OpenMax [14] refines this: for the top-alpha closest prototypes, the activation is downweighted by (1 - Weibull_CDF(distance)), and if the max revised activation falls below a threshold, the sample is classified as unknown. We evaluate OSR performance via AUROC (area under the ROC for the known-vs-unknown binary task) and OSCR (Open-Set Classification Rate, measuring the trade-off between known-class accuracy and unknown rejection rate across thresholds [15]).
future.gcd_description: After OSR rejects unknown samples, they must be grouped into candidate species — a Generalised Category Discovery problem [7]. We use Multi-Granularity Conceptual Experts (MGCE) [17]: three clustering experts operate at different KNN resolutions (k_fine, k_medium, k_coarse), each producing pseudo-labels at a different granularity. A contrastive memory bank aligns representations across scales. The multi-granularity votes are consolidated via InfoMap — a community detection algorithm on a weighted graph that estimates the number of clusters automatically by minimising the description length of a random walk (the map equation). This is particularly suited to botanical data, where the true number of species is unknown and may vary by geographic region.
future.phase3_incremental: Once new species are discovered, the model incorporates them without retraining from scratch: the frozen backbone produces the same embeddings as before; only a new linear classifier head is trained with Cross-Entropy on the augmented label set (known + new species). Because the embedding space is fixed and novel clusters are already well-separated, a 30-epoch fine-tuning of the linear head suffices.
future.phase3_ncd: Our pipeline follows the GCD paradigm introduced by Vaze et al. [7] — their baseline uses a self-supervised pretrained backbone followed by k-means clustering on the novel set. Our contribution extends this in two directions: (1) we replace self-supervised pretraining with supervised contrastive learning (SupCon) to obtain class-aware embeddings that separate known classes while preserving the metric structure needed for novel discovery; (2) we introduce a dedicated OSR stage with OpenMax [14] before clustering, so that novel candidates are filtered from known-class outliers rather than being naively assigned to a known cluster. The spherical orthogonal prototypes [16] further regularise the embedding space, a technique not yet applied to botanical ultra-FGVC to our knowledge.

footer.description: This project is part of a Master's Thesis on the application of Self-Supervised Learning and Novel Class Discovery to biodiversity data.
footer.author: Author: Marcello Russo

exp6.description: The first benchmark establishes the baseline: 6 architectures trained with standard Cross-Entropy loss via 5-fold stratified cross-validation (seed=57). Per-architecture Test F1 results: ResNet-18=0.8799, ResNet-50=0.8822, ConvNeXt-Tiny=0.8902, ConvNeXt-Small=0.8626, DINOv2-Small=0.8883, DINOv2-Base=0.9271. Performance is generally high (macro F1 0.86-0.93), but CE does not explicitly structure the latent space — the objective only penalises misclassification, so same-species embeddings may scatter and different species may overlap. This lack of geometric structure limits two capabilities essential for NCD: (a) detecting out-of-distribution samples (CE softmax scores are known to be overconfident for unknown inputs [15]), and (b) providing a metric space where proximity reflects morphological similarity.

exp7.motivation: From the literature [8] we know that Supervised Contrastive Learning produces more structured embeddings than CE: same-species samples are pulled together, different species are pushed apart. This organized latent space is essential for the subsequent Novel Class Discovery phase [7]. Exp 7 applies SupCon to all 6 architectures with two-phase training: (1) contrastive pretraining of backbone + projection head, (2) CE fine-tuning of the linear head only with frozen backbone.
exp7.title: Exp 7 Analysis — SupCon
exp7.overview: Exp 7 trained 6 architectures with SupCon + CE fine-tuning via 5-fold cross-validation, with final testing on 300 images (50 per species).
exp7.winner: DINOv2-Small dominates the leaderboard with a Test F1 of 0.8958, outperforming the runner-up (ResNet-50, 0.7993) by nearly 10 percentage points. The gap between cross-validation (CV F1 0.9058) and test (0.8958) is only 0.01 — the lowest among all models — indicating excellent generalization. At the species level, it excels on O. sphegodes_Palena (F1=0.990) and O. majellensis (0.980), while the hardest species remains O. sphegodes (0.782). This result confirms DINOv2-Small as the ideal backbone for our domain: lightweight (42M parameters), pre-trained on 142M images, and effectively adaptable via LoRA to 2,232 Ophrys images.
exp7.overfitting: The most striking finding of Exp 7 is the gap between cross-validation and test performance. DINOv2-Base (304M parameters) has a gap of 0.2262 — the worst overall — despite a CV F1 of 0.9135. On O. majellensis, its recall is only 0.12, meaning only 6 out of 50 test images are correctly classified. ConvNeXt-Small (gap 0.1935) and ConvNeXt-Tiny (0.1945) fare similarly poorly. Conversely, ResNet-50 shows a negative gap (-0.0635): its test F1 (0.7993) exceeds CV (0.7359), suggesting that 5-fold cross-validation underestimates its capabilities due to the small validation set size. This pattern suggests that for small datasets, models with fewer parameters and strong implicit regularization generalize better than massive architectures with generic pre-training.
exp7.species: O. sphegodes_Palena is the easiest species overall: DINOv2-Small achieves F1=0.990, ResNet-18 0.960. O. exaltata and O. incubacea are handled well by all models (mean F1 >0.80), likely due to their abundance in the training set (501 and 366 images respectively). O. majellensis is the most polarizing: DINOv2-Small scores F1=0.98, but ConvNeXt-Tiny and ConvNeXt-Small drop to F1=0.21 and 0.25, with recall of 0.12 and 0.14. O. sphegodes is universally the most problematic: no model exceeds F1=0.78, and ConvNeXt precision is below 0.50.
exp7.arch: ResNet-50 and ResNet-18 show the most stable pattern: both have low or negative CV-test gaps, with ResNet-50 reaching 0.7993 despite its relatively simple architecture. ConvNeXt-Tiny (0.6810) and ConvNeXt-Small (0.6886), despite being more modern architectures, perform worse. A possible explanation is that BatchNorm, present in ResNet but absent in ConvNeXt, acts as a critical implicit regularizer for datasets with only a few hundred images per class.

analysis.title: Cross-Experiment Analysis
analysis.description: After training 24 models across four experiments (6 architectures × Exp 6/7/8/9), a systematic analysis of confusion matrices reveals a fundamental limitation of contrastive learning for ultra-fine-grained open-set recognition.
analysis.key_finding: Key Finding: SupCon collapses visually similar species
analysis.key_finding_detail: Cross-entropy (Exp 6) recognizes O. majellensis at 96–100% across all architectures. Switching to SupCon (Exp 7) collapses it with O. sphegodes — accuracy drops to 12–14%. The confusion matrix shows that up to 70% of majellensis images are misclassified as sphegodes. This occurs because SupCon optimizes for embedding similarity, pulling visually near-identical species into the same region of the latent space. The orthogonal prototype repulsion of SpHOR (Exp 8) does not resolve this — results are comparable to plain SupCon. In the NCD scenario (Exp 9), where O. majellensis is the hidden novel class, it is classified as O. sphegodes in 58–90% of cases, explaining the near-random AUROC (~0.5).
analysis.confusion_1: O. majellensis → O. sphegodes: 46–70% in SupCon, 58–90% in NCD
analysis.confusion_2: O. sphegodes → O. exaltata: 8–24% across all experiments
analysis.confusion_3: O. sphegodes → O. garganica: 6–20% across all experiments
analysis.confusion_4: O. sphegodes_Palena → O. sphegodes: 14–42% in SupCon/SpHOR
analysis.root_cause_detail: SupCon pulls same-class embeddings together. For ultra-fine-grained classes where inter-class variance is smaller than intra-class variance (lighting, angle, flower maturity), visually similar but distinct species collapse into overlapping clusters. CE directly optimizes the decision boundary, hence it separates them — but CE embeddings are less structured for clustering and novel-class discovery.
analysis.literature_detail: The Open-Insect benchmark [22], a NeurIPS 2025 spotlight evaluating 38 OSR algorithms on fine-grained species classification, finds that simple post-hoc approaches (Mahalanobis distance, KNN density ratio) consistently outperform complex training-time methods like OpenMax and SpHOR for biodiversity monitoring tasks. This supports our finding that the bottleneck is the embedding space structure, not the scoring function. Additionally, the Multi-Granularity Conceptual Experts (MGCE) framework [17] achieves state-of-the-art on fine-grained Generalized Category Discovery by combining multi-granularity features with dynamic contrastive learning — exactly the direction needed for our domain. Unlike Exp 9 where O. majellensis was the hidden class, Exp 10 includes all 6 species as known and will evaluate NCD on a separate unseen species.

exp10.title: Exp 10 — MGH-NCD (Ultimate Experiment)
exp10.description: MGH-NCD (Multi-Granularity Hard-negative Novel Class Discovery) is the final, definitive experiment of this thesis. It combines four innovations targeting the specific failure modes identified in the cross-experiment analysis. The goal is to maximize both closed-set accuracy and open-set detection (AUROC) for ultra-fine-grained novel class discovery.
exp10.innovation1_detail: The most critical innovation. During SupCon training, the contrastive loss contribution for pairs involving (O. majellensis, O. sphegodes) is multiplied by 5×, and for (O. sphegodes, O. sphegodes_Palena) pairs by 3×. This forces the model to explicitly separate these collapsed species in the embedding space, while maintaining the benefits of contrastive learning for the remaining classes. For Exp 10, all 6 species (including O. majellensis) are known during training. [8]
exp10.innovation2_detail: For ViT-based architectures (DINOv2), features are extracted from three levels: the final CLS token (global semantics), attention-pooled patch tokens (local discriminative details), and the mid-layer CLS token (regional features). For CNN architectures (ResNet, ConvNeXt), features from the penultimate and final stages are concatenated. The concatenated multi-scale vector is projected to a unified 256-dim space via an MLP. This mimics the multi-granularity expert approach proposed in MGCE [17], adapted to our architectures.
exp10.innovation3_detail: An initial attempt at deep fine-tuning (LoRA r=32 + unfreezing last 4 transformer blocks, ~29.5M trainable params) led to severe overfitting: cross-validation F1 reached 0.9266 but test F1 collapsed to 0.1413 (worse than random, 0.167). With only ~1,785 training images per fold, a ratio of ~16,500 parameters per image proved far too high, causing the model to memorize the validation folds instead of learning generalizable features. Phase 2 was therefore reverted to head-only CE fine-tuning (13K parameters, backbone frozen), following the same approach as Exp 7 that consistently generalized well. The backbone is trained with LoRA r=32 during Phase 1 (SupCon), which quadruples adapter capacity for richer embeddings, but is frozen during Phase 2. The head uses LR=0.01 with label smoothing (0.1), Adam, and up to 150 epochs with early stopping (patience=15). [11] This reversal confirms the bias–variance trade-off [18]: on small fine-grained datasets, model capacity must be tightly controlled to prevent overfitting.
exp10.innovation4_detail: OpenMax is replaced by a post-hoc ensemble of three scoring functions, following the findings of Open-Insect [22]:
exp10.innovation4_maha: Mahalanobis distance [21] — class-conditional Gaussian density estimation on the embedding space
exp10.innovation4_knn: KNN density ratio — ratio of distance to nearest known-class neighbors vs. background neighbors
exp10.innovation4_energy: Energy score [20] — log-sum-exp of logits, theoretically aligned with input probability density
exp10.innovation4_ensemble: The final unknown score is a weighted combination: 0.4 × Mahalanobis + 0.3 × KNN + 0.3 × Energy. This ensemble is more robust than any single scoring function.
exp10.outcome_note: All 6 architectures will be trained with the same MGH-NCD recipe for completeness. Unlike Exp 9 where O. majellensis was the hidden class, Exp 10 includes all 6 known species during training. Novel class discovery will be evaluated using a separate unseen species collected for this purpose. Phase 2 uses head-only CE fine-tuning (backbone frozen) for all architectures, following the same approach as Exp 7. The backbone is trained with LoRA r=32 during Phase 1 (SupCon) for richer embeddings. The primary analysis will focus on DINOv2-Base (best tradeoff between embedding quality and GPU memory), with cross-architecture comparisons provided.

research.hero_subtitle: via Deep Learning and Supervised Contrastive Learning
research.hero_university: University of Naples Federico II — DIETI — Master's Degree in Computer Science
research.intro_p1_mid: includes over 300 species of European orchids characterized by an extraordinary morphological similarity that makes their taxonomic identification extremely complex even for expert botanists. This difficulty, known as ultra-fine-grained classification (UFGVC)
research.intro_p1_after: , represents a significant challenge for computer vision systems.
research.intro_p2_before: This thesis addresses the problem by systematically comparing six architectures (ResNet, ConvNeXt, DINOv2) across three learning paradigms: cross-entropy, supervised contrastive learning (SupCon)
research.contrib_1: Multi-architecture benchmark across three learning paradigms
research.contrib_2: Curated dataset of 3,040 images with leakage-free train/test split
research.contrib_3: Latent space analysis via t-SNE projections
research.contrib_4: Open-set evaluation with Mahalanobis, KNN, and Energy techniques
research.dataset_caption: Image distribution per species in training and test splits. The novel species is present only in the test set (548 images).
research.dataset_callout_leakage: In the initial phases (Exp 1–5), the dataset presented a critical data leakage problem: visually identical images appeared in both training and test sets under different filenames. The discovery was made via MD5 content hashing. Starting from Exp 6, the dataset was cleaned using a three-phase protocol: (1) MD5 deduplication, (2) extraction of a balanced hold-out of 50 images per class, (3) stratified 5-fold cross-validation with seed 57. This clean split forms the basis of all experiments.
research.dataset_callout_novel: A seventh species, O. sphegodes_Napoli, was deliberately excluded from the training set and reserved exclusively for testing in Novel Class Discovery and Open-Set Recognition experiments (Exp 8, 10). Morphologically similar to O. sphegodes but with distinct diagnostic characters at the local population level, it constitutes the ideal test for evaluating the system's ability to detect previously unobserved taxonomic entities.
research.dataset_preprocessing: Raw images are processed by a pre-trained Faster R-CNN object detection module that automatically crops the flower by removing the background. Letterbox resize preserves the original aspect ratio with black padding. Input sizes are architecture-native: 256×512 for ResNet, 224×224 for ConvNeXt and DINOv2. During cross-validation, minority classes are oversampled through augmentations (rotations, flip, color jitter, cutout).
